paragraphs: “N—not particularly,” Kolya answered offhandedly. “What ruined my reputation here more than anything was that cursed goose,” he said, turning to Ilusha again. He put on an unconcerned air as he talked, but he still couldn’t control himself, and he kept missing the note he was trying to hold.
“Oh! I heard about the goose!” Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. “They told me, but I didn’t understand it. Did they really take you to court?”

“It was the stupidest, most trivial business. They made a mountain out of a molehill, as they always do,” Kolya began carelessly. “One day I was walking through the market-place here, just as they’d driven in the geese. I stopped and looked at them. Suddenly a fellow who’s an errand-boy at Plotnikov’s now looked at me and said, ‘What are you looking at the geese for?’ I looked at him. He was a stupid, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I’m always on the side of the peasants, you know. I like talking to them.... We’ve fallen behind the peasants—that’s an axiom. I think you’re laughing, Karamazov?”
“No, heaven forbid, I’m listening,” said Alyosha, with a very good-natured air, and the touchy Kolya was reassured at once.

“My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple,” he hurried on again, looking pleased. “I believe in the people, and I’m always glad to give them their due, but I’m not for spoiling them. That’s a _sine qua non_ ... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and said, ‘I’m wondering what the goose is thinking about.’ He looked at me quite blankly. ‘And what is the goose thinking about?’ he asked. ‘Do you see that cart full of oats?’ I said. ‘The oats are dropping out of the sack, and the goose has stuck its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up—do you see?’ ‘I see that perfectly well,’ he said. ‘Well,’ I said, ‘if that cart moved forward a little, would it break the goose’s neck or not?’ ‘It’d be sure to break it,’ he said, grinning all over his face, tremendously pleased. ‘Come on, then,’ I said, ‘let’s try it.’ ‘Let’s,’ he said. It didn’t take us long to arrange it. He stood at the horse’s bridle without being noticed, and I stood to one side to steer the goose. The owner wasn’t looking, he was talking to somebody, so I hardly had to do anything. The goose thrust its head in after the oats by itself, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he tugged at the bridle, and crack! The goose’s neck was broken in half. And, just my luck, all the peasants saw us at that very moment, and they kicked up a row at once. ‘You did that on purpose!’ ‘No, not on purpose.’ ‘Yes, you did, on purpose!’ Well, then they shouted, ‘Take him to the justice of the peace!’ They took me along too. ‘You were there too,’ they said, ‘you helped, everybody in the market knows you!’ And for some reason I really am known all over the market,” Kolya added conceitedly. “We all went off to the justice’s, and they brought the goose along too. The fellow was crying, in a great funk, simply blubbering like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting that you could kill any number of geese that way. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice of the peace settled it in a minute: the farmer was to be paid a rouble for the goose, and the fellow could keep the goose. And he was warned not to play such pranks again. And the fellow kept blubbering like a woman. ‘It wasn’t me,’ he said, ‘he put me up to it,’ and he pointed at me. I answered with perfect composure that I hadn’t put him up to anything, that I had simply stated a general proposition and spoken hypothetically. The justice of the peace smiled and was annoyed with himself at once for smiling. ‘I’ll report you to your masters, so that in future you won’t waste your time on general propositions instead of sitting at your books and learning your lessons.’ He didn’t report me to the masters, that was a joke, but the story got around and reached their ears. They’ve got long ears, you know! The classics master, Kolbasnikov, was especially shocked, but Dardanelov got me off again. Kolbasnikov is savage with everyone now, like a green ass. Did you know, Ilusha, he just got married, and got a dowry of a thousand roubles, and his bride is a regular fright of the first rank and the last degree. The third-class boys wrote an epigram about it:
Startling news has reached our class: Kolbasnikov has turned out an ass.

And so on, awfully funny, I’ll bring it to you later. I’ve nothing to say against Dardanelov. He’s a learned man, there’s no doubt about that. I respect men like that, and it’s not because he stood up for me.”
“But you caught him out about the founders of Troy!” Smurov put in suddenly, plainly proud of Krassotkin at such a moment. He had been especially pleased with the story of the goose.
“Did you really catch him out?” the captain asked, flatteringly. “On the question of who founded Troy? We heard about it, Ilusha told me at the time.”
“He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” put in Ilusha. “He only pretends not to, but really he’s top in every subject....”
Ilusha looked at Kolya with boundless happiness.

“Oh, all that about Troy is nonsense, a trivial matter. I consider it an unimportant question,” said Kolya, with haughty humility. By now he had completely recovered his dignity, though he still felt a little uneasy. He knew he was very excited, and that he had talked about the goose, for instance, with too little reserve, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn’t said a word the whole time. And the vain boy gradually began to be gnawed by a fear that Alyosha was silent because he despised him and thought he was showing off. If he dared to think anything like that, Kolya would—
“I regard the question as quite a trivial one,” he snapped out again, proudly.

“And I know who founded Troy,” said a boy who hadn’t spoken before, suddenly, to everyone’s surprise. He had been silent and seemed shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, called Kartashov. He was sitting near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified amazement.

The truth was that who founded Troy had become a secret for the whole school, a secret that could only be found out by reading Smaragdov, and nobody had Smaragdov but Kolya. One day, when Kolya’s back was turned, Kartashov had hastily opened Smaragdov, which lay among Kolya’s books, and immediately hit on the passage about the founding of Troy. That was a good while ago, but he had felt uneasy and couldn’t bring himself to announce publicly that he too knew who had founded Troy. He was afraid of what might happen, and of Krassotkin somehow putting him to shame over it. But now he couldn’t resist saying it. For weeks he had been longing to.

“Well, who did found it?” asked Kolya, turning to him with haughty superiority. He saw from the boy’s face that he really did know, and at once decided how to take it. There was, so to speak, a jarring note in the general harmony.

“Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilus and Tros,” the boy rapped out at once, and in the same instant he blushed, blushed so that it was painful to look at him. But the boys stared at him, stared at him for a whole minute, and then all the staring eyes turned at once and fixed on Kolya, who was still looking over the daring boy with scornful composure.
“In what sense did they found it?” he condescended to remark at last. “And what does it mean, founding a city or a state? What do they do? Did they each go and lay a brick, do you suppose?”
There was laughter. The offending boy went from pink to crimson. He was silent and on the verge of tears. Kolya held him like that for a minute.

“Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nation, you must first understand what you mean by it,” he lectured him in stern, cutting tones. “But I attach no importance to these old wives’ tales, and I don’t think much of universal history in general,” he added carelessly, addressing the company at large.
“Universal history?” the captain asked, looking almost scared.

“Yes, universal history! It’s the study of mankind’s successive follies and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science,” said Kolya. He was showing off, and he stole a glance at Alyosha. His was the only opinion he was afraid of there. But Alyosha was still silent and still serious. If Alyosha had said a word, it would have stopped him, but Alyosha was silent, and “it might be the silence of contempt,” and that finally irritated Kolya.
“The classical languages too ... they’re simply madness, nothing more. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?”
“I don’t agree,” said Alyosha, with a faint smile.

“The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is simply a police measure. That’s the only reason it was brought into our schools.” Little by little Kolya began to get breathless again. “Latin and Greek were introduced because they’re a bore and because they dull the mind. School was dull before, so what could they do to make it duller? It was senseless enough before, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they thought of Greek and Latin. That’s my opinion, and I hope I never change it,” Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.
“That’s true,” Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing tone of conviction. He had been listening attentively.
“And yet he’s first in Latin himself,” one of the group of boys cried suddenly.
“Yes, father, he says that, and yet he’s first in Latin,” Ilusha echoed.

“What of it?” Kolya felt he had to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. “I’m slogging away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I’d pass my examination, and I think that whatever you do, it’s worth doing well. But in my soul I have a deep contempt for the classics and all that fraud.... You don’t agree, Karamazov?”
“Why ‘fraud’?” Alyosha smiled again.

“Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn’t for the sake of studying the classics that they introduced Latin, but only as a police measure, to dull the intelligence. So what else can you call it but a fraud?”
“Why, who taught you all this?” cried Alyosha, surprised at last.

“In the first place, I’m capable of thinking for myself without being taught. Besides, what I just said about the classics being translated, our teacher Kolbasnikov has said to the whole third class.”
“The doctor has come!” cried Nina, who had been silent until then.

A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov drove up to the gate. The captain, who had been expecting the doctor all morning, rushed headlong out to meet him. “Mamma” pulled herself together and put on a dignified air. Alyosha went up to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. From her invalid chair, Nina watched anxiously as he tidied the bed. The boys hurriedly said goodbye. Some of them promised to come back in the evening. Kolya called Perezvon, and the dog jumped off the bed.
“I won’t go away, I won’t go away,” Kolya said hastily to Ilusha. “I’ll wait in the passage and come back when the doctor’s gone. I’ll come back with Perezvon.”

But by now the doctor had come in, an important-looking person with long dark whiskers and a shiny, clean-shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. As he crossed the threshold he stopped, taken aback. He probably thought he had come to the wrong place. “What is this? Where am I?” he muttered, taking off neither his coat nor his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hanging on a line in the corner, all puzzled him. The captain, bent double, was bowing low before him.
“It’s here, sir, here, sir,” he muttered cringingly. “It’s here, you’ve come to the right place, you were coming to us...”
“Sne-gi-ryov?” the doctor said loudly and pompously. “Mr. Snegiryov—is that you?”
“That’s me, sir!”
“Ah!”

The doctor looked round the room once more with a squeamish air and threw off his coat, showing everyone the grand decoration at his neck. The captain caught the fur coat in the air, and the doctor took off his cap.
“Where is the patient?” he asked emphatically.
